Workshop on Bayesian Workflow

26-27 November 2026

This notebook contains some of the material covered during the two-day Bayesian Workflow workshop at Karolinska Institutet in late November 2026. It is intended for those who are relatively new to Bayesian statistics and the workflow.

The workshop was organized by Simon Steiger, Frida Smids, Paulina Sell and Younes Laalou.
Find more events and information on our website.

Simulation and priors

The first exercise is to simulate a dataset that we can then use to build a statistical model.

Simulating data

We’ll simulate data on air pollution (AP), chronic kidney disease (CKD), age, and systolic blood pressure (BP). The goal is not to make is super realistic, but if the variables and their relationships make a little bit of sense, it’s easier to think about.

In our dataset, exposure to AP increases BP, while having CKD makes this effect stronger. With older age, the risk to develop CKD increases, and so does BP.

Let’s first set up the workspace.

library(rethinking)
set.seed(146)

Air pollution

We start by simulating the independent variables, meaning those that don’t have an arrow pointing at them. These are AP and age. We could imagine different air pollutants here, but we’ll go with a common one: fine particulate matter, PM2.5. mean_PM is the concentration that the simulated values will fall around. We also add noise around that value with rnorm and exponentiate the whole thing so that all simulated AP values are positive.

n <- 1000 # simulating 1000 individuals
mean_PM <- 10
AP <- exp(log(mean_PM) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
summary(AP)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  3.515   8.160  10.058  10.511  12.417  26.525

Age

Simulating age is very straightforward. We use the uniform distribution so that the whole range between 55 and 95 years is covered nicely.

age <- round(runif(n, 55, 95))
summary(age)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   55.0    65.0    75.0    75.2    85.0    95.0

Chronic kidney disease

CKD is next and it depends on age. Older people have a higher risk to develop CKD.

This is why we first set the effect for age on CKD, so how much the risk to develop CKD increases with each year.

b_age_CKD <- 0.3

I set it to 0.3 here, which is definitely not evidence-based :’)

CKD status is binary, so we need to assign yes / no to everybody. And this assignment should be based on the age of each individual. Soo… ??

We first assign a probability to have CKD to everybody.

prob_CKD <- inv_logit(-2.5 + ((age - mean(age)) * b_age_CKD))
prob_CKD[1:5]
[1] 0.534719037 0.002840587 0.386772341 0.738676313 0.123369680

Above, we center the age variable by subtracting the mean from everybody’s age, then we multiply by the effect (b_age_CKD) from above. inv_logit transforms everything to be between 0 and 1 (which we need here, because we want probabilities) and the -2.5 means “not likely” in log-odds space. So the “baseline risk” to have CKD is quite low. (Btw, we set -2.5 by just trying different values and looking at the results which feels weird but it’s okay!)

The next step is more straightforward again, we just sample from a Bernoulli distribution, using the individual probabilities to have CKD.

CKD <- rbern(n, prob_CKD) + 1
table(CKD)
CKD
  1   2 
714 286

By + 1 we make the [0, 1] variable a [1, 2] variable, with 1 being no CKD and 2 being CKD. This is necessary if we don’t want to estimate an offset between the two, but the effects in both CKD groups. We’ll see this in the model code later.

Systolic blood pressure

Now we want to add a blood pressure value for each person in the sample. We first set the effects of age, AP and CKD status on BP as well as an intercept (a_BP) and noise (sigma_BP) for BP.

a_BP <- 110
b_age_BP <- 0.27
b_AP_BP <- c(1.3, 2)
sigma_BP <- 5

b_AP_BP creates the interaction: the effect of air pollution on BP is 1.3 for people without CKD and 2 for people with CKD.

Now we are ready to simulate BP. We sample from a normal distribution again and use the effects we set above together with the variables we have simulated to “modify” the mean. Then we just add a bit of noise and round the results with sigma_BP.

BP <- round(
  rnorm(
    n,
    mean = a_BP +
      b_age_BP * age +
      b_AP_BP[CKD] * AP,
    sd = sigma_BP
  ),
  1
)

The last thing we’ll add is an ID variable.

id <- 1:n

Now we add everything to a dataframe and save it.

data <- data.frame(
  id,
  age,
  BP,
  CKD,
  AP
)

write.csv(data, "data/data.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Plotting the data

Let’s plot the data.

Code 
library(tidyplots)

data <- read.csv("data/data.csv")
data$CKD <- as.factor(data$CKD)

data |>
  tidyplot(x = AP, y = BP, color = CKD) |>
  add_data_points(alpha = 0.7) |>
  # add_curve_fit(method = "lm") |>
  adjust_y_axis_title("systolic blood pressure") |>
  adjust_x_axis_title("air pollution") |>
  adjust_size(width = 90, height = 80) |>
  adjust_font(fontsize = 10)
Code 
data |>
  tidyplot(x = age, y = BP, color = CKD) |>
  add_data_points(alpha = 0.7) |>
  # add_curve_fit(method = "lm") |>
  adjust_y_axis_title("systolic blood pressure") |>
  adjust_x_axis_title("age") |>
  adjust_size(width = 90, height = 80) |>
  adjust_font(fontsize = 10)

Great! Now we can move on to modeling :)

Parameter estimation

Statistical model

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{BP}_i &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma) \\ \mu_i &= \alpha + \beta_{\text{AP}[\text{CKD}[i]]} \text{AP}_i + \beta_{\text{age}} \text{age}_i \\ \alpha &\sim \mathcal{N}(120, 10) \\ \beta_{\text{AP}[j]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(1.5, 2) \\ \beta_{\text{age}} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, 2) \\ \sigma &\sim \operatorname{Exponential}(0.1) \end{aligned} \]

Likelihood

  • \(\text{BP}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma)\): We assume each person’s observed blood pressure comes from a normal distribution. Its centre is \(\mu_i\), the expected BP for person \(i\). \(\sigma\) is the spread, so how far individual values spread around that expectation.

Parameters and priors

  • \(\alpha\) (intercept): The expected BP when AP and age are zero. The prior \(\mathcal{N}(120, 10)\) says that we believe this value is most likely around 120 mmHg.
  • \(\beta_{\text{AP}[j]}\) (air pollution slope by CKD group): The change in BP for each unit increase in AP. The index \(j\) means there are two slopes, one per CKD group. The prior \(\mathcal{N}(1.5, 2)\) expresses the belief that higher pollution increases BP, but it is wide enough to allow no effect or even a negative effect. Both groups get the same prior, but each slope is estimated separately.
  • \(\beta_{\text{age}}\) (age slope): The change in expected BP for each additional year of age.
  • \(\sigma\) (residual standard deviation): How much the individual BP values vary around \(\mu_i\). It must be positive, so we give it an \(\operatorname{Exponential}(0.1)\) prior.

Prior prediction

Let’s check if our priors make sense. We draw 20 values from the priors for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta_{\text{AP}}\). Then we plot all of these lines. This plot tells us which relationships between AP and BP the prior “thinks” are possible.

n <- 20
sim_a <- rnorm(n, 120, 10)
sim_b_AP <- rnorm(n, 1.5, 2)

AP_seq <- seq(from = 1, to = 30, length.out = 30)

plot(
  NULL,
  xlim = c(1, 30),
  ylim = c(80, 160),
  xlab = "air pollution",
  ylab = "blood pressure"
)
for (i in 1:n) {
  mu <- sim_a[i] + sim_b_AP[i] * AP_seq
  lines(AP_seq, mu, lwd = 1, col = "#870052")
}

Looks good!

Now we continue with age and blood pressure:

n <- 20
sim_a <- rnorm(n, 120, 10)
sim_b_age <- rnorm(n, 0, 2)

age_seq <- seq(from = 55, to = 95, length.out = 40)

plot(
  NULL,
  xlim = c(55, 95),
  ylim = c(80, 160),
  xlab = "age",
  ylab = "blood pressure"
)
for (i in 1:n) {
  mu <- sim_a[i] + sim_b_age[i] * age_seq
  lines(age_seq, mu, lwd = 1, col = "#870052")
}

This is not ideal, but okay for our purpose, because we have enough data. We could have improved the prior for age by centering the variable, so that we set it for the mean age (as we did when assigning the probabilities to have CKD). Here, we instead set the prior for a newborn, which is a bit less intuitive and harder to do right.

Fitting the model

Now we are ready to fit the model. Notice how similar the model code is to our simulation code and the statistical model! Once you have these things, it’s really easy to fill out the model.

data <- as.list(read.csv("data/data.csv"))

m_AP_BP <- ulam(
  alist(
    BP ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b_AP_BP[CKD] * AP + b_age_BP * age,
    a ~ dnorm(120, 10),
    b_AP_BP[CKD] ~ dnorm(1.5, 2),
    b_age_BP ~ dnorm(0, 2),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ),
  data = data,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 1000
)

Let’s see whether the model recovered the parameters we set in the simulation!

a_BP       = 110
b_AP_BP    = 1.3, 2
b_age_BP   = 0.27
sigma_BP   = 5
precis(m_AP_BP, depth = 2)
                  mean         sd        5.5%       94.5%     rhat  ess_bulk
a          109.8460670 1.49746736 107.4996491 112.1622251 1.005623  815.0623
b_AP_BP[1]   1.2930506 0.04982536   1.2163884   1.3734349 1.000884  996.1362
b_AP_BP[2]   2.0040922 0.05834193   1.9089519   2.0959306 1.002306  939.9063
b_age_BP     0.2691556 0.01858658   0.2391489   0.2977306 1.006047  745.9896
sigma        5.1011994 0.11559521   4.9236383   5.2968458 1.003084 1355.0469

Isn’t that satisfying <:

Model validation & visualization

Before we explore what we can do with these results, we should look at a few things to make sure the model worked fine. This is of course way more important when working with real data, because we obviously can’t just check if our model found the “real” effects.

Identify issues in estimation

There are a few things we can easily check in every model. These give us hints on whether we can trust the model.

Rhat

In the precis output above, the \(\hat{R}\) value (rhat) indicates whether the four Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains have converged, meaning if they agree with each other. A value of less than 1.01 is generally considered good.
All of our \(\hat{R}\) values are below 1.01, which is good! But of course, a good \(\hat{R}\) value doesn’t mean that the model is right. The chains could converge on the same wrong answer.

Effective Sample Size (ESS)

When the MCMC algorithm moves around the parameter space we want to learn about, each new step (or iteration) is dependent on the last one. This means that the samples we generate are somewhat correlated. The ESS value gives us an idea of how many truly independent samples would give us the same quality of information as the correlated samples. Let’s take one of our parameters, b_age_BP as an example. The ESS for the bulk of the posterior distribution is 746. This means that, in simple terms, our estimate is as good as 746 independent samples. This corresponds to 37% of our total samples, which is good.

Trace Plots

Now we’ll have a look at how the four chains moved around to explore the posteriors of the parameters.

Code 
old_par <- par(xaxt = "n")

traceplot(
  m_AP_BP,
  lwd = 1,
  col = c("#45032c", "#6f0344", "#aa166f", "#eca7c9")
)

par(old_par)

Above, you can see the “history” of the four chains exploring our five parameters. The x -xis shows the iterations. The shaded first half of the sampling process is the warmup phase and is not included in the results. You can see how the chains needed a few iterations just to get to the right region of the posterior. There are smart ways to tell the sampler where it should start sampling, but as you can see, the chains settled on their regions way before warmup was over, so this is okay here.

But in order to judge whether the chains have converged or not, we should “zoom” into the second half of sampling.

Code 
old_par <- par(xaxt = "n")

traceplot(
  m_AP_BP,
  window = c(501, 1000),
  lwd = 1,
  col = c("#45032c", "#6f0344", "#aa166f", "#eca7c9"),
  bg = "white"
)

par(old_par)

This looks like the chains agree with each other. If some of the chains would have been stuck in some region and you could distinguish them from one another, that would be a sign that something went wrong. You can see a few examples of bad looking traceplots here.

Visualize the results

Now let’s visualize our results!

Code 
age_value <- 55 # we plot the line for one age (otherwise we'd need another dimension)

post_samples <- extract.samples(m_AP_BP)

APseq <- seq(from = 1, to = 30, by = 0.5)

n_samples <- length(post_samples$a)
n_x <- length(APseq)

out_noCKD <- matrix(data = NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = n_x)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  out_noCKD[i, ] <- post_samples$a[i] +
    post_samples$b_AP_BP[i, 1] * APseq + # 1 for no CKD
    post_samples$b_age_BP[i] * age_value
}

out_CKD <- matrix(data = NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = n_x)

for (i in 1:n_samples) {
  out_CKD[i, ] <- post_samples$a[i] +
    post_samples$b_AP_BP[i, 2] * APseq + # 1 for no CKD
    post_samples$b_age_BP[i] * age_value
}

summarise_draws <- function(pred_matrix, x_values, prob = 0.95) {
  n_x <- ncol(pred_matrix)

  out_low <- vector(length = n_x)
  out_q25 <- vector(length = n_x)
  out_median <- vector(length = n_x)
  out_q75 <- vector(length = n_x)
  out_high <- vector(length = n_x)

  for (j in 1:n_x) {
    draws_j <- pred_matrix[, j] # all posterior draws for AP value j
    interval_j <- HPDI(draws_j, prob = prob)

    out_median[j] <- median(draws_j)
    out_low[j] <- interval_j[1]
    out_q25[j] <- quantile(draws_j, prob = 0.25)
    out_q75[j] <- quantile(draws_j, prob = 0.75)
    out_high[j] <- interval_j[2]
  }

  data.frame(
    AP = x_values,
    low = out_low,
    q25 = out_q25,
    median = out_median,
    q75 = out_q75,
    high = out_high
  )
}

summary_noCKD <- summarise_draws(out_noCKD, APseq)
summary_CKD <- summarise_draws(out_CKD, APseq)
Code 
plot(
  NULL,
  xlim = range(APseq),
  ylim = range(c(summary_noCKD$low, summary_CKD$high)),
  xlab = "Air pollution",
  ylab = "Predicted BP (mmHg)"
)

shade(
  rbind(summary_noCKD$low, summary_noCKD$high),
  APseq,
  col = col.alpha("cornflowerblue", 0.2)
)
shade(
  rbind(summary_noCKD$q25, summary_noCKD$q75),
  APseq,
  col = col.alpha("cornflowerblue", 0.2)
)
lines(APseq, summary_noCKD$median, col = "cornflowerblue", lwd = 2)

shade(
  rbind(summary_CKD$low, summary_CKD$high),
  APseq,
  col = col.alpha("#870052", 0.2)
)
shade(
  rbind(summary_CKD$q25, summary_CKD$q75),
  APseq,
  col = col.alpha("#870052", 0.2)
)
lines(APseq, summary_CKD$median, col = "#870052", lwd = 2)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c("No CKD", "CKD"),
  col = c("cornflowerblue", "#870052"),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)
